curriculum.lesson_evidence: Data can be biased if the sample leaves people out, questions lead answers, or missing values are ignored. Ask who was counted, who was not, and what the question assumed.
curriculum.scope_limit: Single Stage 4 lesson: partial contribution only. Content-point mapping is pending human review. This authoring pass does not certify NESA alignment.

lesson.child_mission: Data can be biased if the sample leaves people out, questions lead answers, or missing values are ignored. Ask who was counted, who was not, and what the question assumed.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same technology/design idea to a new object or material, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
A poll at the canteen queue asks “Don’t you agree the canteen is too slow?” Why is the question problematic?

FEEDBACK
It leads the answer toward yes and samples only people already waiting — two bias risks.

WATCH FOR
Publishing a big percentage without saying how few people answered.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Rewrite a biased question to a neutral one and name one sample limit you would report.

Write a short reflection naming one observation, criterion or step you corrected and why.

lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Rewrite a biased question to a neutral one and name one sample limit you would report. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Sample: original example using bias on new material; names a specific word, source or choice and explains its effect.

Parent: Written model 2: Sample error: Publishing a big percentage without saying how few people answered.. Correction: It leads the answer toward yes and samples only people already waiting — two bias risks.. Why it helps the audience is stated.

Parent: Likely misconception: Publishing a big percentage without saying how few people answered. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating bias on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with bias, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

Parent: Marking notes: Accept original work about bias with a specific supporting detail. Reject copied model wording with no new material. / Accept a misconception, a correction, and a purpose-linked reason for bias. Reject corrections that do not change the inaccurate idea..

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Surveying only the robotics club about “favourite school subject” biases toward tech interest. A fairer sample includes more groups — or the report must admit the limit.

teach_steps.explain:
Data can be biased if the sample leaves people out, questions lead answers, or missing values are ignored. Ask who was counted, who was not, and what the question assumed.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen, measured or tested against criteria.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties, criteria or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer. For practical technology work, follow teacher safety rules for tools, food and devices.
